questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with painless ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. On examination, it is indurated with a clean base and non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark field microscopy shows motile spirochetes. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) is caused by Treponema pallidum. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose is the first-line treatment. Dark field microscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis of primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches over the forearm for 1 year. Slit skin smear shows 2 bacilli per oil immersion field (BI = 2+). Skin biopsy shows granuloma with lymphocytic cuffing but no bacilli. What is the classification of this leprosy?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy: BI of 1-2+, multiple hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, histology shows granuloma with lymphocytic cuffing but bacilli may be absent or sparse in skin lesions. Nerve damage and asymmetry are features. TT has BI 0 and single lesion.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompromised man develops painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome. He also develops ipsilateral uveitis and ear pain. Which antiviral is most appropriate?
opts: Acyclovir 400mg five times daily for 7 days
Valacyclovir 1000mg three times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 250mg three times daily for 7 days
Acyclovir IV 10mg/kg every 8 hours for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster with ocular involvement (ophthalmic branch) and ear involvement (Ramsay Hunt syndrome features) in an immunocompromised patient warrants IV acyclovir to prevent dissemination and serious complications. Oral antivirals are used for immunocompetent patients.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with chronic indolent ulcer over the lower leg for 6 months. Biopsy shows large encapsulated yeast cells with a thick polysaccharide capsule forming narrow-based budding. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Cryptococcus neoformans shows large encapsulated yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule and narrow-based budding on histopathology. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals. Primary cutaneous cryptococcosis is rare but can present as ulcers.

questions.q: A patient with pemphigus vulgaris has been on prednisolone 60mg/day for 3 months. New lesions continue to appear. The next step in management is:
questions.exp: Rituximab is now considered first-line therapy for refractory pemphigus vulgaris (unresponsive to conventional steroid therapy). Anti-CD20 therapy depletes B-cells and reduces desmoglein antibody production. It has been shown to be superior to conventional treatment in randomized trials.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and polyarthritis for 3 months. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA is elevated. Which skin finding is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus lesions (scarring, follicular plugging, atrophy) when found in a patient with SLE are highly specific. While malar rash is classic, it is not specific as it can occur in rosacea and other conditions. Discoid lesions, when biopsied, show interface dermatitis with mucin deposits.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with gradually enlarging mole on her back. Dermoscopy reveals an atypical pigment network, irregular dots and globules, and regression areas. Biopsy shows malignant melanocytes with a Breslow depth of 1.8mm and no ulceration. What is the recommended surgical margin?
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness 1-2mm, the recommended surgical excision margin is 2 cm. For melanoma <1mm: 1 cm margin; 1-2mm: 2 cm margin; >2mm: 2-3 cm margin. Breslow thickness is the most important prognostic factor for primary cutaneous melanoma.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with pruritic, tense bullae on normal skin and on urticarial plaques for 2 months. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid targets BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1). BP180 is the major target antigen. Linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ on DIF is diagnostic. Desmoglein 3 is targeted in pemphigus vulgaris; laminin 332 in mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with tinea capitis showing kerion formation. Culture shows macroconidia with 6 cells, thick walls, and echinulate surface. Which dermatophyte is most likely?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis produces large, spindle-shaped macroconidia (8-15 cells) with thick, echinulate walls and a pointed tip. It is zoophilic (cats and dogs are reservoirs) and causes ectothrix infection. Kerion is an inflammatory reaction to dermatophyte infection.

questions.q: A neonate presents with bilateral eyelid swelling and purulent discharge 3 days after birth. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. What is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Ophthalmia neonatorum due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae presents on day 2-5 as purulent conjunctivitis. Gram stain shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci. Treatment is ceftriaxone 25-50mg/kg IV/IM as a single dose. Chlamydial ophthalmia (day 5-14) is treated with systemic erythromycin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old patient presents with a pigmented lesion on the sole showing a streak from the nail fold to the free edge of the nail (Hutchinson's sign). Dermoscopy shows irregular parallel ridge pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) is the most common melanoma subtype in Asians and Africans. Hutchinson's sign (pigment extending to the nail fold), irregular parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy, and acral location are characteristic. It has the worst prognosis among melanoma subtypes.

questions.q: A 70-year-old patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops purpuric lesions on the lower legs that are palpable. Biopsy shows fibrinoid necrosis of small vessel walls with neutrophilic infiltrate and nuclear dust. What is the histological term for this finding?
questions.exp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) is characterized histologically by fibrinoid necrosis of small vessel walls, neutrophilic infiltrate, and leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust from neutrophil fragmentation). Clinically, it presents as palpable purpura. IgA-LCV is Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy on multidrug therapy develops sudden onset fever, painful erythematous nodules all over the body, and iridocyclitis. ESR is elevated and biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate in dermis with no granulomas. What is this reaction called?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (Type 2 reaction) occurs in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic involvement. Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate with immune complex deposition.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with hyperkeratotic plaques over the elbows, knees, and scalp with silvery scaling. Nail shows oil drop sign, pitting, and onycholysis. The Auspitz sign is positive. Which cytokine pathway is primarily involved in psoriasis pathogenesis?
questions.exp: The IL-17/IL-23 axis is central to psoriasis pathogenesis. IL-23 (from dendritic cells) drives Th17 differentiation, which produces IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22. These promote keratinocyte proliferation and recruitment of neutrophils. Biologics targeting IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and IL-23 (guselkumab, risankizumab) are highly effective.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with multiple flesh-coloured papules around the mouth, nose, and eyes since adolescence. Histology shows stellate fibrosis and entrapped hair follicles and adnexal structures. Which genodermatosis is this associated with?
questions.exp: Trichilemmomas are hamartomas of the outer root sheath of hair follicles, pathognomonic of Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome). Cowden syndrome is associated with breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer. Angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum) around the nose is seen in tuberous sclerosis.

questions.q: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation develops intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques starting on the abdomen (sparing the umbilicus) and spreading to limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPPP) is the most common pregnancy dermatosis. It begins within striae in the third trimester, spares the umbilicus, and resolves after delivery with no fetal risk. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically and targets BP180. ICP presents with palmoplantar pruritus and elevated bile acids.

questions.q: A patient undergoes patch testing. Reaction is read at 48 hours (+) and 96 hours (++). The sensitizer causing the reaction is identified as potassium dichromate. What is the type of hypersensitivity reaction in allergic contact dermatitis?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV (delayed/cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. In the sensitization phase, antigen is presented by Langerhans cells to T-cells. On re-exposure, memory T-cells release cytokines causing inflammation 48-96 hours later. Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old farmer presents with verrucous plaques on the dorsum of the foot after a thorn prick 2 years ago. Biopsy shows muriform (sclerotic/Medlar) bodies. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is caused by dematiaceous (melanin-containing) fungi, most commonly Fonsecaea pedrosoi. Pathognomonic finding is muriform bodies (Medlar bodies/copper pennies) - round, thick-walled, brown, septate cells in tissue. Trauma inoculation in tropical regions is the route.

questions.q: A 38-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with rapidly growing cauliflower-like vascular nodules on the skin and oral mucosa. Warthin-Starry stain of the biopsy reveals gram-negative bacilli in clusters. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) in immunocompromised patients. It mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but Warthin-Starry silver stain shows clusters of gram-negative bacilli. Treatment is azithromycin or doxycycline for 3 months. KS is caused by HHV-8 and shows spindle cells.

questions.q: A newborn presents with widespread blistering at birth with features of skin fragility. Electron microscopy shows cleavage through the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. Mutations are in which protein?
questions.exp: Junctional EB with cleavage through lamina lucida (between basal keratinocytes and lamina densa) is caused by mutations in laminin 332 (laminin 5), integrin α6β4, or BP180 (type XVII collagen). Integrin α6β4 mutations cause Junctional EB with pyloric atresia. Type VII collagen mutations cause Dystrophic EB (sub-lamina densa cleavage).

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss over 6 months following a major surgery. Trichoscopy shows a predominance of telogen hairs with short vellus hairs and multiple empty follicles. Hair pull test is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium follows a precipitating event (surgery, childbirth, illness, stress) by 2-3 months (the telogen lag period). Diffuse hair shedding occurs as hairs prematurely enter telogen. Hair pull test is positive (>3 hairs). Anagen effluvium (from chemotherapy) is immediate and more severe. Trichoscopy shows increased telogen:anagen ratio.

questions.q: A patient develops blistering at sites of minor trauma and milia formation. Biopsy shows sub-epidermal bulla. Indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin shows IgG deposits on the dermal floor of the blister. Which condition is this?
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is an acquired autoimmune blistering disorder with IgG antibodies against type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils). On salt-split skin, IgG deposits on the dermal floor (unlike BP which is on the epidermal roof). Milia formation is a classic feature due to the deep level of blistering.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with depigmented patches on the face and hands showing hyperpigmented borders. Wood's lamp examination shows chalky white fluorescence. Histopathology shows absence of melanocytes. What is the treatment option with the highest repigmentation efficacy?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy is the most widely used and effective treatment for generalized vitiligo, achieving repigmentation in 60-70% of patients. It is safer than PUVA (no systemic psoralen side effects). Excimer laser is more effective for localized, stable vitiligo. Tacrolimus is effective for facial vitiligo.

questions.q: A 55-year-old chronic smoker presents with a non-healing ulcer at the vermilion border of the lower lip for 4 months. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which precursor lesion most commonly precedes lip SCC?
questions.exp: Actinic cheilitis (solar cheilitis) is the most common precursor of squamous cell carcinoma of the lip, caused by cumulative UV exposure and tobacco use. Features include blurring of vermilion border, scaly plaques, and ulceration. Treatment options include vermilionectomy, topical 5-FU, and laser ablation.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with diffuse systemic sclerosis develops painful, dusky-coloured fingers upon cold exposure that turn white, then blue, then red. What is the correct sequence of colour changes in Raynaud's phenomenon?
questions.exp: Raynaud's phenomenon: triphasic colour change - White (vasospasm/ischemia) → Blue (cyanosis from deoxygenation) → Red (reactive hyperemia on rewarming). It affects fingers, toes, nose, and ears. In SSc, Raynaud's is often the presenting symptom and can be severe enough to cause digital ulcers and gangrene.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with flesh-coloured papules with a central dell on the chest and axilla of an immunocompetent patient. Electron microscopy of the characteristic cell inclusion shows ovoid, brick-shaped virions. Which family does the causative virus belong to?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the Poxviridae family. EM shows large brick-shaped/ovoid virions. Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies are the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusions on light microscopy. In immunocompromised patients, lesions are larger, more numerous, and atypical.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient is prescribed isotretinoin for severe nodulo-cystic acne. Which of the following monitoring tests is NOT routinely required before starting isotretinoin?
questions.exp: Before starting isotretinoin, baseline monitoring includes: pregnancy test (female patients), serum triglycerides and cholesterol, liver function tests, and CBC. Urinalysis is not a routine requirement. Monthly monitoring during therapy includes pregnancy test, triglycerides, and LFTs. Isotretinoin is teratogenic (Category X) and causes hypertriglyceridemia and hepatotoxicity.

questions.q: A 65-year-old diabetic man develops rapidly progressing painful cellulitis on the foot that spreads to the leg within 24 hours. Crepitus is felt on palpation. Blood culture grows gram-positive cocci in chains. What is the diagnosis and causative organism?
opts: Necrotizing fasciitis Type II - Streptococcus pyogenes
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis Type II (monomicrobial) is caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) - gram-positive cocci in chains. It presents with rapid progression, severe pain disproportionate to findings, crepitus, and skin necrosis. Treatment: emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin + clindamycin (to inhibit toxin production).

questions.q: A patient with chronic plaque psoriasis requires phototherapy. Which wavelength of narrowband UVB is most effective for psoriasis?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB at 311-313 nm (Philips TL-01 lamp) is the most effective wavelength for psoriasis phototherapy. It specifically targets the action spectrum for psoriasis while minimizing erythemogenic wavelengths (290-300 nm). It is superior to broadband UVB and comparable to PUVA, without the side effects of psoralens.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with thick yellow-brown nails showing transverse ridging, subungual hyperkeratosis, and a proximal extension of the hyponychium. The nail is friable and crumbles. KOH of nail clippings shows dermatophyte hyphae. Which nail structure is affected in distal subungual onychomycosis (DLSO)?
questions.exp: Distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO) is the most common pattern (80%) caused by Trichophyton rubrum. Infection begins at the hyponychium (distal nail bed), spreading proximally under the nail plate, causing onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis. The nail matrix is uninvolved, preserving nail formation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with multiple, well-circumscribed, round patches of non-scarring alopecia on the scalp. Trichoscopy shows exclamation mark hairs and yellow dots. The patient has a strong family history of thyroid disease. Which HLA type is associated with alopecia areata?
questions.exp: Alopecia areata is associated with HLA-DQ3 (DQB1*03) and HLA-DR11 (DRB1*1104). It is a T-cell mediated autoimmune condition targeting the hair follicle. Exclamation mark hairs (tapered at base, thicker distally) and yellow dots on trichoscopy are diagnostic. Association with thyroid autoimmunity, vitiligo, and Down syndrome exists.
